questions.question: Explain why African leaders formed the SANNC in 1912.
questions.expected_answer: By 1910 Africans had lost most of their land and independence, and the Union of 31 May 1910 created a Parliament that only white men could sit in, with no African vote outside the Cape, where the qualified franchise was under threat. The new government planned laws on land, labour and passes. African political organisations were regional and easy to ignore. The South African Native Convention of 1909 and the delegation with W. P. Schreiner to London in 1909 failed to change the constitution but showed that leaders from different regions could work together. Educated leaders who believed in constitutional rights felt betrayed because race, not education or property, became the test of rights. Pixley ka Isaka Seme called for a national congress to overcome ethnic and regional divisions, and the SANNC was formed to unite Africans and give them one national voice.

questions.question: Describe the founding conference of 8 January 1912 and the first leaders of the SANNC.
questions.expected_answer: The conference was organised by Pixley ka Isaka Seme, a lawyer trained at Columbia, Oxford and in London, and met in Bloemfontein on 8 January 1912. Several hundred delegates attended, including chiefs, lawyers, teachers, ministers, journalists and representatives from Basutoland, Bechuanaland and Swaziland. Seme said that white people had formed a Union in which Africans had no voice, so Africans must form their own union. John Langalibalele Dube was elected president in his absence, Sol Plaatje secretary-general and Seme treasurer, and an upper house of chiefs was included. The organisation was renamed the African National Congress in 1923. Women were not full members until 1943, though they organised separately, for example against passes in 1913 and in the Bantu Women's League led by Charlotte Maxeke from 1918.

questions.question: Describe the aims and methods of the early SANNC and evaluate how successful they were.
questions.expected_answer: The SANNC aimed to unite Africans across ethnic and regional lines, defend their rights, oppose discriminatory laws and speak to the government for African people. It used peaceful, constitutional methods: petitions, deputations, letters to newspapers, public meetings, its newspaper Abantu-Batho and delegations to London. Its first major campaign was against the Natives Land Act of 1913; a delegation of Dube, Plaatje, Rubusana, Msane and Mapikela went to London in 1914, but Britain refused to intervene because South Africa was self-governing, and Plaatje wrote Native Life in South Africa (1916). In the short term these methods failed to stop discriminatory laws, and critics said the Congress was too cautious and distant from workers and rural people. But it created a national African identity and organisation that lasted, became the ANC in 1923 and later grew into a mass movement that won the 1994 election.
